speechtext:
The house resumed from Monday, March 4, consideration of the proposed motion of Mr. W oodsworth:
That, in the opinion of this house, no disposition of the natural resources, under the control of the federal government, shall be effective until ratified by parliament.
And on the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Guthrie:
That the motion be amended by striking out the words "natural .resources" where they occur in said motion and by inserting in lieu thereof the words "water-powers".
Hon. H.H. STEVENS (Vancouver Centre): Mr. Speaker, the motion before the house is a very brief one. I shall read it in order to keep fresh in the minds of hon. members the subject matter of the discussion which has been engaging our attention now for several days:
That, in the opinion of this house, no disposition of the natural resources, under the control of the federal government, shall be effective until ratified by parliament.
To that a very modest amendment has been moved, limiting the words "natural resources" to water-powers. On this motion and amendment there has been very considerable discussion.
I would like at once to remind the house, as many hon. members have done, that this resolution is in very broad general terms. I do not wish, however, to join with some hon. members who have attacked the hon. member
[Mr. Gott 1
for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) who moved the original resolution, and to say that there was any ulterior design in expressing the resolution in such general terms, because I believe that what was in his mind was to introduce a resolution which would be of a character to enable members of this house to declare themselves on the principle which he had in his mind, and I think we should give the hon. member credit for sincerity in so far as that is concerned.
But I do differ with the hon. member, and I have felt myself in some difficulty from the commencement of this debate, in regard to the precise application of this resolution to the administration of the public affairs there referred to by a government, irrespective of what that government might be. I think, when a resolution of this kind is introduced into the house, the general tendency of parliament is to receive it in the spirit in which it is offered, and not to be too critical in the interpretation one puts upon it. Very frequently resolutions of this character are passed by this house, and they are not interpreted as directing the government to give effect to the exact letter of the resolution, but rather, the resolution serves as a general guide for the government. But in this case, the government, represented by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart), whose department was particularly affected, has attacked the resolution rather vigorously; in fact, I think we had four or five ministers yesterday expressing their views on the resolution.
There is enunciated in the resolution a principle which I think meets with fairly general support, and that is that within reason the public should keep control of these natural resources, such as water powers. Where we differ is as to the exact method of control. Some hon. members would have the water powers of Canada entirely under government direction and administration. Others are prepared to keep control of them in a measure, but to allow certain latitude to private enterprise. However, there has been a marked difference of opinion. A little later on, I desire to offer to the house an amendment which I hope will meet with general approval, and will in a sense break the deadlock which we have witnessed in the discussion so far, an amendment which I think will bring even my hon. friends on the government benches to its support.
But let me first bring to the attention of the government, and more particularly of my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior, just what precipitated this discussion, just what was behind the introduction of this resolution. I do not wish to be discourteous to the minister. It is customary, when you are going to

Natural Resources-Mr. Stevens
offer some criticism of a minister's action, to tell him first that you think very highly of him. I shall not do that other than by this implication. He understands me, I think, sufficiently to make it unnecessary for me to indulge in those courtesies, but I do wish to say to him this: Last year on the 6th day of June, the Minister of the Interior, speaking from his seat in the house, and representing the government, gave certain assurances to parliament in reply to a rather pointed request made by the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). I wish to read briefly some extracts from what the minister said on that occasion, and then I want to say to him that in the light of those statements which he made, he surely must realize that parliament is justified in criticizing him for-what shall I say?-at least not carrying out the spirit of his observations of last year; I think I can put it in that way. The minister said on that occasion, and this was in reference to a request I had made of him a couple of years ago regarding Spray lakes, that such resources " should not be alienated but be put under the control of parliament." He was referring there to the resources in the national parks. I want to bring this to the attention of the minister and of parliament right at this point. Yesterday the minister told us that the government had under way at the present time a process, by legislation or by regulation, of taking Spray lakes outside of the boundaries of the parks, and then they would be able to deal with them. I would suggest to the minister that that is scarcely keeping faith with his promise to parliament that these resources should not be alienated without consulting parliament.

Now I understand my hon. friend to say that if I give a pro-mise that no disposition of any water-power will be made until it is placed under the control of

Mr. Bennett interrupted and said, No. The discussion continued:
Mr. Stewart (Edmonton) : What did my hon.
friend say?
Mr. Bennett: I said we should not part with any water-powers without the approval of this parliament.

Mr. Bennett: Or approval of a contract given by resolution.
Then Mr. Stewart goes on:
-and now a very grave difference of opinion exists with respect to the disposition of the Seven Sisters falls. I may assure my hon. friend that until that difference of opinion is settled I am not going to issue any license for that water-power. I think I may assure my hon. friend of that.
In regard to the license given for that water-power or to the action of the Manitoba government in granting whatever licenses it had power to grant, I have no criticism to offer because I am not in a position to say whether it was a provident contract or not. That is a question for the people of Manitoba to determine; I am not going to discuss it. But I say to the minister, whether his promise was in regard to the Seven Sisters falls or the Spray lakes or anything else, a promise given by a minister of the crown from his seat in this house should not only be observed in its general terms, it should be observed to the very letter. In other words, a ministerial promise ought to go even further than what might be squeezed out of the interpretation of its words. And it is because certain members of parliament, in fact a substantial number, feel that parliament has not been treated quite fairly and courteously in this regard that this debate has been precipitated. I suggest that a salutary lesson has been read not only to the present government but to future governments that it is not wise-shall I say?-to play with parliament in matters of this kind.
Now, as this debate has proceeded some difficulties have been disclosed. The Minister of the Interior tells parliament this year, as he did last year, that he has been the storm centre for some years in regard to dealing with the natural resources, particularly I think, those of Manitoba.

Now I come to my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell). He is not in his seat. He told us yesterday that the whole proposal to divide water-powers from the other natural resources, as suggested

Natural Resources-Mr. Stevens
by the amendment now before the house, is utterly ridiculous. The Minister of Agriculture, with his usual faculty for burlesquing something in opposition to which he cannot present sound reasons, made fun and sport of the whole business-in marked contrast to the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning), who, with his customary vigour, argued along another line. The Minister of Agriculture asks, whoever beard of a government doing such a thing as is proposed? Whoever heard, he wants to know, of a government separating one resource from another in administration. Let me read exactly what he said:
How can. we justify segregating water-powers and deciding that they shall be dealt with in the particular manner .provided by the amendment to the resolution, leaving all other resources to be administered as they have been for the last half century or more?
He goes on-and I would direct the attention of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to this:
No government could justify making that distinction and legislating thereon.
I will show in a moment that this government has for ten years administered affairs just in that way; I will prove that conclusively. So that the Minister of Agriculture added nothing to the debate by ridiculing what his government is already doing.
The Minister of Railways was very much alarmed because, as he said, if this resolution were carried in its original form a prospector might be operating on the boundary line between Alberta and British Columbia, and not knowing precisely where on that mountainside the boundary line came he might find himself compelled to come to parliament if he happened to be on one side, or to go to Victoria if he happened to be on the other side.

I would not introduce chat question had the Prime Minister not gone to such an elaborate extent in dealing with the natural resources question, and had he not so emphasized the rights of the provinces, not only in this matter but in others as well. He deemed it his duty to uphold the great doctrine of provincial rights. Now here we have before the government-not, I would remind him, before parliament-what is perhaps one of the largest questions with which this country has been faced in many years, namely, the granting of approval to the Beauharnois power scheme. speechtext:
I listened to the debate yesterday, and I have had the privilege of reading the debates of the previous days. I believe in the principle of ministerial responsibility to parliament; the principle of legislative responsibility on the part of parliament and of ministerial responsibility in administration in order to give efficient and practical application to such legislation as parliament may enact; and in the further principle that in so far as powers are vested in the governor in council to be exercised in their sole discretion, they have the right to exercise that discretion subject to their being amenable to parliament. If I were called upon to decide as to whether the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) had exercised a proper discretion in granting the license for the Seven Sisters falls power site, I would be unable to do so because I am not in possession of sufficient information. If the issue is that of a condemnation of the Minister of the Interior, in justice to him and in justice to parliament it should be brought forward by a substantive original motion, or by proposing an amendment when we are on the motion to go into committee of supply or committe of ways and means. In that manner all the facts relevant and pertinent to the exercise of that discretion by the minister could be discussed by parliament upon the amendment then before the house, and we would be in position to deal with the issue on its merits.
I was somewhat embarrassed by the nature of the original resolution, and to a lesser extent by the amendment. I would have voted for the amendment as it stood, but would have done so simply as an expression of opinion on the part of the house, to the effect that, even although it may be within the jurisdiction of the governor in council to deal with certain matters by order in council, there are 78594-43
times when such matters are of such supreme importance to the whole country that parliament should be taken into the confidence of the government before a final disposition is made of the matter.
I had some personal experience with regard to the administration of the act of 1912, which vested in the province of British Columbia the administration of water-powers. When that act was first passed by this house it was provided that orders in council passed by the legislature of British Columbia in reference to the carrying out of the act should retain validity and force only until the close of the next succeeding session of the parliament of Canada, when, if they were not approved by the parliament of Canada, they became invalid and of no force or effect. The wide scope of that amendment brought before the parliament of Canada not only the granting of the original license or permit, but all such minor modificartdons or amendments as were necessary for the carrying out of the original undertaking. However, it was found that the administration of the Water Powers Act of British Columbia was made impossible when every minor matter connected therewith could only become permanently effective on receiving the approval of the parliament of Canada. I brought that to the attention of the government of the day, and the clause providing that every order in council should be brought before parliament for its approval was repealed, because it was found impossible to administer the affairs of the country under such a provision.
The debate has disclosed that the Minister of the Interior, in the exercise of his discretion in reporting to the governor in council and the governor in council in granting the permit or license for the development of water-power at the Seven Sisters falls, if that is the name, acted clearly within the well-defined limits of the powers vested in the minister and the governor in council by the act which has been under discussion, chapter 210 of the revised statutes, an act respecting Dominion water-powers. But we find that the minister, in carrying out the duties imposed upon him, not only consulted with his colleagues in the government but found it necessary, in view of the importance of that undertaking, to consult with certain members of the house, some fourteen in all, if that is the number. My contention is that if the minister in the exercise of his discretion finds it necessary, on a matter of the disposal of natural resources, the water-powers of the country, to consult ten or fourteen members, it is a matter of such importance that he should frankly come to the whole house, be-



Natural Resources-Mr. Cahan
cause each one of us as an individual member has exactly the same responsibilities as the members from Manitoba with whom he did consult.
Therefore, there are, as the circumstances have disclosed, exceptional cases when the house should be consulted with respect thereto. If I had voted for the original amendment, as I intended to do, I should have voted for it with the explanation that I think it is too broad in its terms and as merely indicating that there are circumstances which are peculiar, conditions which are special, which at certain times render it advisable that the government, before vesting these water-powers in companies or in private individuals, should consult the house with regard to their prospective action, so that there may be a clear discussion, a clear vision in the minds of the members as to what is involved, and so that the practical approval of the house may be obtained before such concessions are made. Had I voted for the amendment, I would not have voted as condemning the Minister of the Interior. He acted within the clearly defined jurisdiction vested in him by the act to which I have referred and that act, chapter 210 of the revised statutes, dealing with water-powers, was an act introduced into this parliament by the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen as a government measure when he was Minister of the Interior and was, after certain amendments, supported unanimously by the house. Therefore if it were shown that the Minister of the Interior had acted honestly, with no wrongful intent or corrupt motive, I would not be prepared to condemn him for exercising the power vested in him by an act of parliament which received the unanimous approval at least of this bouse.
But we have by a resolution which we passed the other day unanimously agreed that the natural resources of the three provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta should be vested in those provinces respectively, that is, vested in the crown as representing the three provinces respectively. Until that is carried out there must be a certain provisional period, and some temporary arrangements must be made, because it is essential to the administration of public affairs in this country that under our institutions ministerial responsibility should be maintained. Therefore I am not personally in favour of continuing a condition of affairs in which the Minister of the Interior, in exercising his duties as vested in him by an act of parliament, shall be in a position to come before the house and justify his action

by reason of the fact that he has secured the prior consent of the government of a province. The government of the Dominion must be responsible to parliament; the government of Manitoba, Saskatchewan or Alberta must be responsible to the appropriate legislature. Therefore I think, as a provisional measure, the amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) should receive the unanimous support of the house, because until the transfer of the natural resources is made to these provinces respectively, it provisionally places the administration of the water-powers of Manitoba under the control of the legislature and government of that province, and the same in respect of the water-powers of Saskatchewan and Alberta. That is a temporary solution of the difficulties with which we are confronted.
I have had some practical experience over a period of years dealing with the development of water-powers. I was the executive head for seven years of the development in another country of one of the largest and most magnificent water-powers ever known. My experience is that in dealing with the development of water-powers it is impossible that every petty change in plans or specifications, or even a change of site or a change in the conditions under which the operations take place, should always, necessarily, receive the ratification of the legislative assembly or the parliament which is in legislative control. I could give a dozen such experiences showing the impossibility of bringing these matters up for legislative ratification. They must be left as matters of administration, and the government must remain responsible to parliament for their administration, the proficiency, the honesty of it. Therefore I suggest that this is a fair solution, because I firmly believe the development of water-powers should be left to the legislature and government of the province in which those water-powers exist.
If I might be permitted to refer to Beau-harnois, I think the rights of the province of Quebec are clear with respect to the development of the so-called Beauharnois power on the St. Lawrence river. I have read in the press the questions and the answers given thereto by the supreme court on a recent reference, but I have not yet seen published in the press a full statement of the reasons embodied in the opinion of the court. I have heard it said inside and outside of parliament that it seemed to convey no clear idea as to the respective powers of Ontario and Quebec on the one hand, and the Dominion on the other. But after having read that

Furthermore, I think the opinion of the supreme court gives to those of us who are anxious to see a reasonable and equitable settlement of the question of the development of power on the St. Lawrence river a basis of compromise that will be acceptable to the whole country. When this project was first discussed, it was proposed that the power development and the navigation development should be made by the government of Canada under the terms of a treaty to be negotiated with the United States. I believe that if the government had undertaken to carry out that policy, they would have met with great disfavour in all the provinces except Ontario and Quebec, because I have been from almost one end of the country to the other since that suggestion was made, and if I am able to gauge public opinion, public opinion in the maritime provinces and public opinion in the west is against this government undertaking a national liability of $300,000,000 or more for the purpose of developing cheap power for Ontario and cheap power for Quebec at the expense of all the rest of the country. But as it is clear from the opinion given by the supreme court that the province of Ontario, owning the bed of the river St. Lawrence to the boundary line, and being invested with the power rights and privileges, except those which pertain to the riparian owners, has under its legislative jurisdiction the development of power from the Canadian shore of that waterway, I think it is far better that that province should be left to carry on that development by such public-ownership methods or system as it desires to adopt.
Further, I entirely approve of the suggestion made by the Prime Minister the other

Natural Resources-Mr. Cahan
day, if I understood him right., that he had decided, I presume in view of this opinion, to take the governments of Ontario and Quebec into consultation in order that together they might come to a unanimous agreement with regard to the exercise of their respective rights in the St. Lawrence river, whether as to the international section or the Quebec section. That removes one of the most aggravating causes of irritation and discord that would otherwise exist throughout the length and breadth of this land.
If I am not going beyond the question, I would like to make this suggestion to the Prime Minister. I have been accustomed ro read engineers' reports. I have lived ten or twelve years of my life in daily consultation with some of the best hydro-electric engineers that could be procured either on the continent of Europe or in this country, and I have read each one of the reports that have been made on the development of the St. Lawrence river from earliest times down to the present. I would suggest to the right hon. gentleman that there is a method whereby we could preserve for all time, on the Canadian side of the river, a thoroughfare for navigation that would not be dependent in any respect on the legislative jurisdiction of the state of New York or of the congress of the United States, or be dependent on administration by the government of the state of New York or by congress itself.
I reject at once, in such opinion as I have, the idea of developing the international section of the river by one great dam south of Barnhart island. No volume of water such as that was ever contained by one dam, and there is no reason why we should enter upon the experiment. But if you make a dam at the foot either of Crysler island or near Ogden island across the river, which could only be done by agreement between the two countries, you bank up the water and form what is practically a great lake above the dam which will be of a depth suited for navigation. If you build another dam at the foot of Barnhart island you back up the water to such a depth that you have practically a new lake running away back for several miles. The plans which have been so far suggested provide for locks on the American side to drop down at Ogden island and looks, also on the American side, to drop down at Barnhart island. The plans provide further for a weir on the American side which will control the flow of the river, so necessary to maintain the proper levels at the city of Montreal, in which I am particularly interested. But what is worse, those plans provide for one powerhouse, one-

Now, I tell the Prime Minister, this country will never agree to have those locks and those weirs and that powerhouse entirely upon American soil. I believe that is the almost unanimous opinion of the public, as I come in contact with it. But it is easy to overcome that difficulty, and if this matter is to be further investigated I think the board's engineers should ascertain, as it is possible to put locks on the American side to enable the ascent from one level to the other, whether it is not also quite feasible and practicable to put locks on the Canadian side to fulfil the same functions at a not very extreme cost; and weirs should be placed on the Canadian side to control the flow of the river, so that for all time to come, while we accept the treaty pledges of the United States with the utmost confidence, we will alleviate all anxiety on the part of Canadian shipping that they may be compelled at certain times of stress to pass through American locks in order to proceed from the St. Lawrence up into the Great lakes. As a provision against that possibility the extra expense is entitled to very favourable consideration.

That, in the opinion of this house, no disposition of the natural resources, under the control of the federal government, shall be effective until ratified by parliament.
To this two amendments were moved, which were declared to be out of order. Then another amendment was proposed that the
words, "natural resources" be changed to "water-powers". Finally we have the amendment now under consideration.
It would seem to me, Mr. Speaker, that hon. gentlemen opposite have been arguing for three or four days in favour of taking more and more precautions in guarding our heritage of natural resources, particularly water-power sites; but that in supporting the last amendment they are arguing directly opposite, that is, to lessen the precautions. The hon. member (Mr. Stevens) who moved the amendment very kindly said he was coming to the aid of the members on this side to get them out of their dilemma. I hold that we are not in any dilemma, for I am quite convinced that we are on sound ground in opposing the amendment.
As the debate has been in progress for several days my observations will be very brief. At the present time six of the provinces have their natural resources, and negotiations are now pending having in view the transfer of their natural resources to the other three provinces. This has been the condition for a long time, and it may continue for a long time yet. We have had legal discussions as to the relative positions of the Dominion and the provinces in regard to water-power sites. In a general way, my understanding is that within the province controlling its own natural resources the provincial authority has jurisdiction over the banks and the bed of water courses, but that any navigation features are under the control of the federal authority. Surely it was never intended that the Dominion government should take advantage of that in order to interfere with- or impede or retard waterpower development. Within the provinces that have not their natural resources, this government would have control of all. So that the amendment simply means that the three provinces that have not their natural resources will have to come to this parliament before they can make use of their waterpower sites, whereas the six provinces who now have their natural resources will be able to go ahead and develop them in the interests of their own people. That, I claim, is not only an inferior but a humiliating position; and I claim further that it puts some of the provinces under the protetting wing of this parliament.
The members of the provincial legislatures have an opportunity to travel around their provinces and become acquainted with local conditions; they are in a position to decide what measures should be taken in regard to

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I
refer to the amendment to the amendment may I say a word with respect to a matter of procedure in this house in connection with amendments. It is customary, when amendments are being proposed from the opposite side of the house or when important motions are to be introduced to which the government is expected to make an immediate reply, that in advance the government will be supplied with a copy of the proposed amendment or motion. I do not say for a moment that my hon. friend, who has presented the amendment we are now considering and who is an old parliamentarian, intended in any way to overlook that practice; I am sure it was a mere oversight on his part, but since he intimated in his remarks that his desire was to find some common ground on which all members of the house could unite I think it would have facilitated what he had in view if before beginning his remarks he had intimated that he would move an amendment, and had in advance supplied the government with a copy of it. Hon. members will see in a moment that especially where reference is made to some statute passed years ago with special application to a particular province, the government cannot be expected, having a sense of its responsibility in matters of this kind, to accept immediately and in an offhand way a suggestion which may involve many factors not apparent, on the surface, and to which some thought and consideration must necessarily be given. I would suggest to hon. members that this practice, which is one of the oldest of parliamentary usages, should be followed on all occasions vrhere the desire is not to take the government unawares for the purpose of obtaining some snap verdict, but rather for the purpose of having a deliberate opinion expressed by those who are responsible.

Natural Resources-Mr. Mackenzie King
May I say a word with regard to the amendment to the amendment. The original motion was a very broad one in its application; it related to the disposition of all natural resources. It soon became aparent, both to the mover of the motion (Mr. Woodsworth) and to hon. gentlemen opposite who have spoken in support of it, that they had gone much too far; that as a matter of fact they were advocating something which they had come to see was really unwise and unworkable. They began a retreat and sought to discover some means of gracefully accomplishing that retreat; at that stage the acting leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie) came forward to extricate his forces and introduced an amendment which limited very considerably the scope of the original motion. Instead of a further consideration of all natural resources, the acting leader of the opposition brought in an amendment which limited the subject matter to water-powers. That was a considerable step backward from the original motion which had been receiving the support of hon. gentlemen opposite. But my hon. friend (Mr. Guthrie) after he had brought forward his amendment discovered that he too had gone too far, and 'began to look around for a chance again to retreat. It was not the members on this side of the house who were ini a dilemma, as the hon. member for Toronto West Centre (Mr. Hocken) has suggested; it was the acting leader of the opposition who found that he had introduced an amendment which was against the interests of the western provinces. Between yesterday and to-day he and the members of his party have 'been in conference as to how they could get out of the particular predicament into which they had fallen through that amendment. So in order to help the acting leader of the opposition out of his difficulty, the horn, member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), his left bower at the moment, comes along with an amendment to the amendment. That is a unique spectacle, if I may use a word which has been adapted more than once in this debate;- we have the acting leader of the opposition declaring a policy and then we have one of his followers asking, with his consent, that this parliament do. not accept the policy which the acting leader has put forward but accept something much less important and significant.
We sympathize with the hon. gentlemen in their dilemma and we will go as far as we can to help them out. We are as anxious as they are to have this matter settled in a manner which may meet if that is possible, with unanimity in this house. So long as
the house understands exactly what it is being committed to, there is no reason why we should not be in agreement with respect to the amendment to the amendment which has been moved by the member for Vancouver Centre. This amendment brings us back to the position this government has been asserting all along. My hon. friend (Mr. Stevens) drew attention to the fact that we had been stressing provincial rights, had been stressing the right of the provinces of the Dominion to their own resources and that we were seeking to have those resources administered by the provinces as speedily as possible. He says to us, "That being the case, why will you' not accept my amendment? it only asks you to do that much." I may say to my hon. friend that we are prepared to accept his amendment if that is the significance of it, but in accepting it I want to have a distinct understanding with the house as to just exactly what we are accepting so that there will be no misunderstanding later on and the onus placed on the wrong shoulders with respect to the consequences of certain phases in the legislation which my hon. friend is anxious we should accept.
May I read one or two significant clauses in the Railway Belt Water Act so that hon. members will see exactly what is being proposed. Subsection 2 of section 5 of the act, which is chapter 211 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, reads as follows:
2. Subject to the property in and the rights to the use of water referred to in subsection one hereof,	_	_
(a) all water without distinction within the railway belt shall, during the pleasure of the governor in council, for the purposes of administration be under the control of the authorities of the province of British Columbia and be administered under and in accordance with the water acts, as if the said acts were enacted by the parliament of Canada subject to the provisions of this act, and the officers and authorities having powers and duties to exercise and perform under the provisions of the water acts shall have the like powers and authority with respect to or in connection with the administration of the said water,
Section 7 of the act reads as follows:
The governor in council may, at any time, repeal the provisions of section five of this act, by proclamation to be published in the Canada Gazette, and upon the repeal of the said section. the water shall be administered under regulations to be made by the governor in council.
I wish to direct the attention of the house to the fact that this legislation begins and ends with action by the governor in council. If we should accept this act, I do not wish to be told by hon. gentlemen opposite that we are proceeding to govern by orders in

They have been condemning us day after day for doing certain things under orders in council and now come along and ask us to accept an act which contains provisions that certain things shall be subject to the action and approval of the governor in council. Let me repeat, if we accept this act, I do not want hon. gentlemen to say, when we act under it, that we are proceeding under orders in council and that instead we should be coming to parliament for some ratification which the act says nothing about.
My hon. friend (Mr. Stewart) has mentioned that at the time this act was passed certain provincial acts for the administration of water-powers within the province were in effect; also that there was a certain area referred to in this particular act, the railway belt, which was under the control of the Dominion government. In so far as the water-powers in that particular area were concerned, this act took them from under the control of the federal government and transferred them to the province of British Columbia to be administered under the water acts of that province. My hon. friend suggests that similar provision should now be made with respect to water-powers in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. I must direct his attention to the fact that at the present moment those prov-vinces have no water acts under which they could administer these resources; they will have to legislate in order to give themselves authority to administer these water-powers once they come under their control. That is the reason the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) instead of the government of Manitoba had to act with regard to the lease of the Seven Sisters falls; the Manitoba government could not take these resources, administer them and give the contract which was necessary as it had not the existent powers required to administer the resources as would have been the case had Manitoba had water acts similar to those which the province of British Columbia had prior to the time this act was passed. In accepting this amendment we must not be asked to tie up the whole development of the 'western power resources in the interval between this moment and the time at which the provinces pass the necessary legislation in the nature of water acts to give them the power of administration which they will require.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my right hon.
friend (Mr. Mackenzie King) in opening his remarks this afternoon seemed to think that I am in some kind of a dilemma in respect of the amendment I moved in the house last Thursday. I can only say that I do not find myself in any dilemma whatever in regard to that amendment. That amendment was drawn as an amendment to the main motion as it then stood, a motion which I did not approve, as in my judgment it went too far. By that amendment I limited the application of the motion as presented to the house by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) and the principle embraced in the amendment I moved is, I am satisfied, absolutely sound.
My right hon. friend is wrong in another surmise, that in some way I, as temporary leader of the Conservative party in the house, have been a party to framing a subamendment in order to get myself out of some dilemma. That is pure surmise on the part of my right hon. friend. I am free to admit this-and under other similar circumstances I would admit it-that at any time a new proposal is presented to me, as it was in this case this afternoon by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), as one that might meet with the approval of the house, I have no hesitation in saying that I will accept it under those circumstances. Indeed I think it is my duty to do so; and I may add that I had had no prior consultation with the hon. member for Vancouver Centre when he brought this matter to my attention before the meeting of the house this afternoon. I think it is a better proposal than that embodied either in the motion or in my amendment, a more workable one and one that achieves the end we seek in regard to this matter.
What have we overcome? The principle which has been acted upon by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) in the instance spoken of most frequently during the course of the debate is in my judgment an improper principle. It may be justified by the law of the country as it stands to-day; nevertheless that law is in my opinion founded upon an improper principle. Why should the Minister of the Interior be permitted on a matter of great public importance to be carrying on, unknown to this parliament, what is a

Natural Resources-Mr. Guthrie
secret negotiation or arrangement with the government of a province of the Dominion, in breach of a very strong assurance which the minister himself gave to this house on the 6th of June of last year? Our objection is that these negotiations are carried on secretly by one government with another, under the guise of orders in council, and that, in my opinion, is a pernicious principle when any part of the public domain of this country is involved. Our aim was, so far as it was possible, to stop further operations by this government or by any minister of this government in respect to these natural resources which the Dominion still owns and controls. The object sought to be achieved by the subamendment is to allow the legislatures of the three provinces named in the subamendment to have execlusive control of these natural resources when they are transferred to the provinces.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
I wish to say a few words on the amendment to the amendment. The Prime Minister has made a declaration of policy but what this parliament needs is a bonfire made of the Dominion Water Power Act and to recover control by parliament of this work. There will be no cheap power for the people of this country so long as that act remains in existence. The Prime Minister has burned his bridges behind him. He seems to do everything by fits and starts, and nothing long on this water-power question. The other day when the question of water-powers was being discussed he abandoned as a waif and orphan and outcast the St. Lawrence waterway and the power that is to be developed therefrom. He seems to have a new policy for every hour of the day with something new to promise and employ. As a public-ownership supporter for some thirty years in the province of Ontario, I want to tell you that you are just going around in a circle by all these acts. The Railway Belt Water Act, chapter 211 of the statutes of 1927 relating to British Columbia, has been on the statute books since 1912, but it is not legislative enactments and decisions by the courts that give cheap light and power to the people of this country. It is the men who are behind the enterprise. This parliament has been going around in a circle during this past week with regard to this particular proposition. The original resolution deals with the natural resources, while the amendment deals only with water-powers. The time has come for this parliament to have charge of the granting of these water-powers.

Natural Resources-Mr. Church
If the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) has been guilty of an error, it was an error of judgment. Do not let us blame the minister; let us blame parliament. The Dominion Water Powers Act is twenty-five years behind the times. The annual report of the Department of the Interior for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1928, states on page 110:
On January 1, 1928, the total water-wheel and tumbine installation throughout the Dominion amounted to 4,777,921 horse-power or only a little more than 11 per cent of the possible development. A very conservative estimate places the capital investment in the generation, transmission, and distribution at $875,000,000, a sum greater than that invested in any other single manufacturing industry in Canada.
An analysis of the utilization of the present installation indicates that
(1)	3,904,678 horse-power, or 81-7 per cent of the total, is installed in central electric stations for general public distribution.
(2)	528,731 horse-power, or 11-1 per cent, is installed in pulp and paper mills which, in addition, use power purchased from the central electric stations to the extent of approximately
775.000	horse-power.
(3)	344,512 horse-power, or 7-2 per cent, is installed in_ general industrial enterprise for electro-chemical reduction, manufacturing lumber. flour milling and other purposes.
The fact that the high average of 502 horsepower of hydraulic installation is available per
1.000	of population, is significant in an era when the industrial prosperity of a county is so closely linked with the amount of mechanical power available to its workers, and in this rega'rd Canada occupies a most advantageous position amongst the countries of the world.
New installation during 1927 amounted to 221,655 horse-power, or a little less than during 1926. This figure gives no indication of the intense activity in hydro-electric construction during the year which will result in an additional installation of about 378,000 horse-power being completed by midsummer of 1928, whilst other developments upon which construction has begun or is about to begin will, it is anticipated, increase the installation by a further 2,000,000 horse-power by the end of 1930.
It is up to this house and parliament to adopt a new policy with regard to the granting of water-powers. Only eleven per cent of the power Canada possesses is yet developed. Change our policy before it is too late.
The subamendment of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) is very good as far as it goes. It provides that the prairie provinces shall have light and power laws of their own making after the fashion of the Railway Belt Water Act, 1912. I shall support the amendment on the ground that it means home rule for the western provinces. It will get way from the old policy that has prevailed in the past of the administration of these natural resources by a department of this government. It is the only proper policy to give to the three prairie provinces their water-powers free of all restrictions, and let them
lay down a hydro-electric policy of their own along the lines of the Ontario system in conjunction and in partnership with the municipalities. There is no doubt that the Prime Minister has grasped at this subamendment like a drowning man at a straw and has burned his bridges behind him to stem the tide of criticism over the bungle made of the Seven Sisters site.
Might I ask the Prime Minister if it is also proposed to adopt the suggestion of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) with regard to the Beauhamois project and immediately issue a permit? That project will destroy the whole hydro-electric system in the province of Ontario. The province of Ontario is to get power at the rate of $15 per horse-power, but at the end of the contract the price will be raised sky-high and may be nearer $40 or $50 per horse-power, and while a few dollars may be saved to-day, it will cost the province in years to come many millions of dollars to get a ransom and freedom.
Yesterday the hon. member for North Vancouver (Mr. McRae) characterized the exploitation of water-power sites in the United States as the crime of the century. Undoubtedly he is right. There was a great fight in Los Angeles between conflicting interests over the development of cheap light and power, and the legislature of California was compelled to pass a statute to control the development of water-powers and regulate the earnings and rates of the power companies. That should be done here. The people want the government to lay down a policy. Every session for the past seven years we have had battles in this house on this power question, and I have brought forward the power question in an attempt for seven years to get the government to declare its policy. In 1924 the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario applied for the right to develop and generate power at Morrisburg, an application similar to that made by the Beauhamois interests, but the government declined to grant the commission license to proceed. The hydro forces were routed in the battle of the Morrisburg dam. In 1927 this government was repulsed on the Ottawa river in what is known as the battle of the Carillon. For six weeks the government did not know whether they were for the Sifton proposal or against it. The government were not only repulsed, they were routed and put to flight in that particular Carillon battle. Last session the government were nearly defeated in what is known as the first battle of the Beauhamois, when the yeas were 54
6S6

Natural Resources-Mr. Church
and the nays 58 on my motion for the six-months' hoist of that proposition. We are looking for another battle along the same lines. Now there has been a fight in Winnipeg, and the Bracken government has capitulated.
The second battle of the Seven Sisters falls and the third battle of the Beauharnois power site will be carried to the polls, because it is the electors who are going to settle these questions. The principle involved will not be settled by the Prime Minister running away from a declaration of policy. This battle will be decided in the polling booths, and the people are going to demand that for all time there shall be a national waterpower policy for each province. As far as I can see, the Liberal party has deserted its principles in its treatment of the natural resources of the western provinces. The members of that party must take full responsibility before the electorate for their failure to compel the government to lay down a policy regarding cheap light and power. Where does the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke) stand on this question? He is the only cabinet minister from Manitoba. Is he in favour of public ownership in his province? In the last election the party now led by Premier Bracken appealed to the people on a public ownership policy, but they were not twenty-four hours in office before they threw overboard their principles and pledges, and surrendered to the Winnipeg Electric Company. And where does the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) stand on this particular question? After all, cheap light and power means more to the toiler than to anybody else. Both the Minister of Labour and his colleague the Minister of Immigration have yet to be heard from. The Backuses, the Holts, the Gundys, the Joneses, the Sweezeys and the other financial barons can all come down to parliament and get away with the water-powers of the country over parliament's head and many of the people. Why, the hon. gentleman from St. Lawrenee-St. George (Mr. Cahan) propose to give some of them the Beauharnois power site.
We are told that this parliament is not concerned, that the government is absolute, and that parliament has no more to do with it than the pyramids of Egypt. Well, whatever may be said in favour of the party system, I think it has not maintained the prestige of this house on this power question. The decay of our influence has been particularly noticeable during the past few weeks. The House of Commons in Canada is becoming not a ruling body, let alone a critical body.

Ministers who now rule are in reality not ministers of the crown. The rigidity of the party system has marked the decay of the House of Commons. The party that wins a majority Obtains automatically absolute control regardless of the wishes of the crown or of the country. As the franchise is more and more extended the party machinery has also been strengthened with the attendant result of the decay of parliament and of parliamentary institutions. In some of the provinces even the opposition in reality exists in name only and we have a one-man legislature, whose word is law and the assembly is powerless. The commission system has also deprived parliament of a lot of its powers and prerogatives mostly for the gain of selfish interests. Canada has just got a new status without the authority or knowledge or consent of the electorate.
The granting of the license to the Winnipeg Electric Company to develop the Seven Sisters water-power site has been justified by those in favour of it, or at least they have attempted to justify its alienation by pointing to the report of Doctor T. H. Hogg. I cannot understand how the Hydro-Electric Commission of Ontario, a public ownership body, released Doctor Hogg for any such purpose. In the olden days every child knew who was the chairman of that commission, but now you have to consult a directory to find out. Sir Adam Beck was the champion of public ownership, and every official of the commission had to follow him. To-day the chairman has slept at his post, and for two or three years past there has been no active support of Sir Adam Beck's policy. The chairman has refused to fight the battles of public ownership, and he let the engineer of the commission, Doctor Hogg, recommend the handing over of the Seven Sisters power site to a private corporation. Let me say to Doctor Hogg that he cannot serve two masters in this Seven Sisters proposition. He is described as Doctor Hogg. Well, the first prescription he issued in Manitoba has about electrocuted the Bracken cabinet, and it may have something to do with the electrocution in the next election of some hon. gentlemen opposite from that province. The west has little to hope for from the Prime Minister regarding a solution of the coal question or the railway question. The government have made a political football of the coal question in the west, they have made a political football of the natural resources of this country, .now they are making a political football of

Natural Resources-Mr. Church
this water-power proposition. I have very little hope of any solution of the question from that quarter.
The amendment is on the principle that if the House of Commons is not to lose its influence as a representative institution no disposition of the natural resources under the control of the federal government shall be effective until ratified by parliament. Only by asserting legislative control over our natural resources will it be possible to prevent their exploitation by powerful monopolies. The present family compact in this regard in my opinion is worse than the family compact of 1837. It may be urged that the terms of the present contracts with these monopolistic power companies are favourable to the consumers of electric current, but I fear when the time comes for those contracts to be renewed such prohibitive rates will be insisted on as will cripple the industrial development of this country, and the labour of generations yet unborn will be adversely affected and mortgaged.
To-day the west instead of being exclusively agricultural is fast becoming an industrial country. The extension of hydraulic power in Manitoba will be a great boon in providing cheap light and power. It is not intended for the city man alone; it is intended for the farmer, the housewife, the toiler, and the worker in every industrial centre. The extension of cheap light and power will serve to retain the rural population, it will assist in the work the good roads movement is doing, and it will help to solve rural economic problems. It is the means to the end of solving the troublesome question of men, money and markets. A low cost of hydraulic power, for city and farmer alike, means better homes, higher standards of living, reduced hours of labour, improved health and happiness, better crops and generally improved conditions. Cheap light and power would bring about a revolution in agriculture and would greatly improve conditions of labour on the farm. It would make for the joy of living on the farm. It would be a genuine boon to the farmer who is now ground down under long hours of strenuous labour, and who is faced periodically with bad times and poor prices. The question of farm relief is uppermost in the United States to-day as well as in this country, and one cannot emphasize too strongly the benefits to be derived from a proper system of hydraulic power when extended by rural lines to the farm at cost.
I have here a table showing what can be accomplished by man-power and machinery to-day in agricultural development. This table
is taken from the bulletin of the National City bank of New York for December, 1928, and the facts it discloses are quite illuminating. There is also in the bulletin an article by Professor E. A. Stewart of the State Agricultural college of Minnesota, in which this writer shows what has been done by means of cheap light and power and modern machinery in that great state for the farmers, who are now operating under improved conditions. The article shows the effect of cheap light and power in the matter of economy, improved prices and the solution of the very vexed question of depopulation in rural communities.
The province of Manitoba is ito-day in the position which Ontario occupied in 1905. At that time the last concession of 20,000 horsepower in the Niagara river was given away by the Ross government. Sir James Whitney then came in and, with Sir Adam Beck, launched the hydro movement, with the result that 868,000 horse-power are developed on the Niagara river to-day for the use of the people. A similar boon the province of Manitoba could have to-morrow if it adopted a sound hydro policy. What is needed not only in Manitoba but in Saskatchewan and Alberta as well is a proper municipal hydro policy for the development of hydro-electric power along the lines I suggest. But instead of taking steps in that direction this government is content to give away the water-powers of the country to private interests, making millionaires out of some people at the expense of the population at large-and this without the consent of parliament. In this case the government is acting without the consent of the legislature of Manitoba or of this parliament.
I am bound to say that I am very much ' dissatisfied with the whole policy of this government not only in connection with the Seven Sisters falls but also with respect to the Beauharnois power scheme, the Chicago diversion, and the administration of the Water Powers Act. I contend that a bonfire should be made of the Water Powers Act which is fifty years out of date, and a new policy adopted by parliament, so that the executive should no longer rule but that this parliament should decide upon what terms and conditions leases ought to be granted with respect to these water-powers, which are the property of the people of Canada. There has never been a country on the face of the globe so rich in water-powers as the Dominion of Canada. Yet only 11 per cent of this power is developed, 89 per cent being undeveloped. I say, there was never a country for which

Natural Resources-Mr. Church
Providence has done so much and1 man so little; Providence has given us a great heritage, but we are doing nothing to preserve that heritage for the people who are to come.
The Ontario hydro-electric policy, or pattern, I urge, should be extended to the three prairie provinces, giving them home rule in this respect. And this is largely a labour policy. More than that, it is a protectionist policy. But in this regard,, as in other respects, hon, gentlemen opposite are free traders; they believe in giving away the property of the Canadian people, as Santa Claus gives away toys from the Christmas tree. They have been giving away to their favourites the water-powers that belong to the people of this country. I repeat, the hydro-electric policy which we have in Ontario is a protection policy. Sir Adam Beck fought the battle of the masses against the classes in Ontario, protecting the masses of the people of that province against their oppressors, the light and power grabbers. He redeemed the province of Ontario from the slavery of high cost light and power, in the real sense of those terms, by giving them cheap light and power and transportation as well at cost. That is what will have to be done in Manitoba, and' tomorrow in Saskatchewan and Alberta as well. The Tolmie government out on the Pacific coast has also, a great opportunity with regard to cheap light and power if it will only adopt a hydro-electric policy in that great province, which gets so little from this government. It will make for a greater industrial Pacific province. The hope of that province is in the Tolmie administration. They will not be found wanting.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) professes to have a great regard for the working man, but he utterly ignores the policy of the Labour people; forgetting their principles, he supports a policy like this, the object of which is merely to hand over to private interests the property of the people of Canada, without let or hindrance. The policy of the government in relation to this matter marks the decline of parliament, and it shows us how badly this country stands in need of a new policy for the development of our water-powers. The Minister of Labour describes himself as a deep sea diver. Well, may I point out to him that the principles of liberalism, about which we hear so much to-day, were long ago dumped on the scrap heap and have now been consigned like McGinty to the bottom of the sea. In the action of the government with reference to the Seven Sisters falls the minister, along with his colleagues, has thrown overboard all the principles of true liberalism

and of labour. I ask the Minister of Labour now-he says he is a deep sea diver-to go down to the bottom of the sea and rescue those principles. Let him bring them up from the dark unfathomed caves of ocean and get his party and the government to do something with them.
The Minister of Labour is fond of making addresses in behalf of Labour. What has he done in this great war declared against the rights of the people in the matter of water-powers? Was he lined up with those who were concerned in protecting the working classes in Winnipeg and the farmers of Manitoba when these particular water-powers at the Seven Sisters were handed over, over the heads of the people's representatives? Was he opposing the surrender of these rights to private interests who wish to exploit them for greed and gain?
The people of Manitoba will not be really prosperous until their water-powers are conserved for their own use. The labour man in that province as well as in Ontario and Quebec pays not only the cost of his light and power but also interest on a capitalization of millions of dollars. Now what is the situation with respec't to the Beauharno'is proposition? The Prime Minister-if he does not run away to-morrow from what he said yesterday-proposes to give the Beauhamois people a permit under the Navigable Waters Protection Act. It has been said, of course, that parliament can intervene, by section 12 of that act, and revoke the permit. I contend that parliament cannot do so. A private bill will have to be introduced, and it will go to the foot of the list for the session after its first reading. When the contract is completed it will cost them tens of millions of dollars, because then the Beauhamois people will raise their rate for direct current. That is what happened in the Niagara district when the "big clean-up" deal was put through; the city of Toronto had to pay $32,000,000 to rescue the citizens of Toronto from the clutches of the privately-owned power companies. In the Financial Post of Toronto, shortly after Sir Adam Beck's death, appeared the following:
Beck died at the height of a public ownership movement that swept him into a position of power and mastery that no other man in Canada has held. The hydro will likely disintegrate as a single institution into a number of smaller corporations, some publicly, and in time, many privately owned, but all linked in a superpower chain.
Is that what is to become of the investment of $300,000,000 made by the people of Ontario

Natural Resources-Mr. Church
if they link up with the Beauharnois power movement set out so fully by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George?
Reference has been made to new Ontario; why is it that new Ontario is controlled by private corporations to-day? The reason is that in 1907, 1908 and 1909, Sir Adam Beck and the hydro municipalities wanted Sir James Whitney to bring the joy of cheap light and power to the mining camps of that country, and electrify the Temiskaming and Northern railway, but he did not see fit to do so, with the result that private corporations from the United States gained control of that whole mining country and kept new Ontario back twenty-five years. Instead of our present silver production of about $18,000,000 and gold production of about $16,000,000, together with a very small population, if hydro had gone into that territory we would have a population now of about a half to three-quarters of a million with a gold: and silver production of over $100,000,000 a year. Now the Ferguson government 'has to go into northern Ontario and buy out many of these private companies and pay a huge sum to do so.

I simply give this as an illustration of what happens when we allow private corporations to control these utilities. That has been the experience of new Ontario; to-morrow it will happen with reference to the Beauharnois development, and the day after to-morrow this will be the result of the Seven Sisters lease. If these privately-owned corporations are allowed to go on in this way, the day will come in the prairies and elsewhere to buy them out, and the people will pay.
The Minister of Public Works has heard the Beauharnois case, but he was not allowed to sit alone; he was provided with two official guardians, one of them being the Minister of the Interior who has handed over the Seven Sisters site to the Winnipeg Electric Company and its friends. No doubt we will hear in a few days that the Beauharnois proposition has been passed over the head of parliament, and there is no use saying parliament can revoke a license once given. As the leader of the opposition pointed out the other night parliament cannot revoke a water-power permit without, as I say, being brought into the exchequer court and forced to pay damages for the loss sustained by the private company as they will have vested rights. Then the argument was advanced that under section 12 of the Navigable Waters Protection Act these 7S594-44
licenses can be cancelled. I have a bill under that section ready to introduce as soon as this permit is granted; all I can do is to bring in.a bill saying that the order in council is hereby annulled, but that bill will be read a first time and then go to the bottom of the list.
Last session the government were asked to lay on the table of the house all papers in connection with the Beauharnois scheme; that request was repeated this year, but those papers have not yet been brought down and those re the Seven Sisters site only at the beginning of last week. So far as the people of this country are concerned, as the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Ryckman) has said, the whole question of water-powers some day or other must be decided by the privy council. That is one court where we can get some decision as to the division of authority as between the federal and provincial governments. As my hon. friend pointed out, before the Supreme Court of Canada, counsel for the Dominion contended there was no water-power in Canada on any navigable stream which the Dominion could not expropriate without paying compensation, and could develop it and sell this power to the people. These questions will have to be decided sooner or later; it has been pointed out already that the questions put to the supreme court were not properly drawn; they should have been framed jointly by the Dominion and the provinces, and in any event this question will have to go eventually to the privy council. There is no use in passing additional legislation; some private company affected by this legislation will take the question to the privy council eventually and you will not make any headway with regard to water-powers until the court of last resort -has laid down under the British North America Act what are the separate powers and rights of -the Dominion and the provinces. No question is settled until it -is settled aright rather than making a football of things to kill time till after the next elections are over.
If the central provinces of Canada do not wish to develop and generate power themselves I think it would be good politics for hon. gentlemen opposite to adopt a national hydro-electric policy on the St. Lawrence from canal works in order to protect the working people in central Canada from paying rates on millions of dollars of invested capital held by private corporations, and sell this power at cost to the two provinces. In my opinion a decision of -that kind would be in the public interest, because I have very little faith in anything being done with regard

Private Bills

to the preservation, and conservation of these water-powers for the whole people not only-in central Canada but in the west as well. We have seen how this works in the United States; the late President Roosevelt pointed out how the water-powers had been frittered away, and he stated that posterity would have to pay millions of dollars to regain them. I think the example of Ontario in the light and power movement should serve as an illustration to the three western provinces. The twenty-five years of cheap light and power which Ontario enjoyed is an example to the other provinces of the Dominion. The only way to learn anything with regard to the light and power situation is from example and not by adopting the mistakes which have been made by some of the older provinces. Some of them have parted with their water-powers in the same way that Santa Claus hands out presents from the Christmas tree. Ontario provides a lesson on the results of a forward hydro policy for the prairie provinces. The net results in Ontario I sum up' as follows:
In these paragraphs we have the result of what the Hydro-Electric has done:
1.	Every dollar of the $160,000,000 hydro investment is earning interest and sinking fund.
2.	Hydro investment saved Ontario from a coal famine that would have bankrupt the province in war time.
3.	Hydro investment saved 2,200,000 shareholders over $75,000,000 in reduced coal, light and power bills.
4.	Hydro investment saved Ontario over $100,000,000 on coal prices, which would have gone ix>
$30 per ton in war time but for the hydro investment that gave Ontario the equivalent of 3,000,000 tons of United States coal per annum.
That is what was accomplished in Ontario, and we should endeavour to see that the water-powers of the country are preserved for posterity.
The amendment of the acting leader of the opposition is such that the executive or administrative side of the government would no longer have control of the parting with these magnificent water-powers, but parliament should recover the same and conserve them for the people.

(Mr. C. H. DICKIE (Nanaimo) moved the second reading of Bill No. 62 respecting the Esquimalt and Nanaimo Railway Company.
Explain.

Mr. Speaker, by this bill the Esquimalt and Nanaimo Railway Company seek an extension of time for building a couple of branch lines on Vancouver island. I know of no reason why the bill should not be allowed to proceed. As you know, Sir, these branch lines are built as the requirements of the timber trade demand their construction. In the past there was no particular occasion to build these lines, but today with the increased forestry business of British Columbia they are necessary. The Canadian National Railway system is nowhere near the district to be served by these two lines. In fact, in railway parlance, it may be said to be Canadian Pacific territory. No other railway interest would be prejudiced in any way, and I cannot understand why there would be any objection to granting the extension of time.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words on this bill. The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Dickie) in moving the second reading says he does not know any reason why thp bill should not be passed. I presume his point of view is merely that of one acting for the company and wishing to get the bill through. The 78594-444
proposed branch lines are some hundred miles away from his district; in fact they are entirely in the western portion of my riding, and he will therefore perhaps pardon me if I take a few minutes to discuss the bill more from the angle of the people of the district affected than that of the company behind it.
I may say that personally I am entirely in favour of the building of these branch railways, and I am quite sure that I speak also for every man and woman in that portion of .the district affected. But, sir, when I say we are entirely in favour of the building of the proposed railways, and also entirely in favour of this bill, it is with this proviso, that we be satisfied that the passing of the bill and the building of the branch lines are one and the same thing, and not a means of tying up this country for another five, and possibly another ten, years. The original act was passed in 1919, so the promoters already have had ten years to carry out their plans.
Now, I see one or two points in this bill that I should like to mention. First, it contains no provision for the work to commence within two years of the passing of the bill: simply the promoters are given five yeai'3 within which to complete the work. That is a departure from the ordinary practice. I have before me Bill No. 41, introduced by the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Kellner), and it covers a number of branch lines, some fourteen I think, to be built by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. I may say that the bill now before us, while ostensibly in the name of the Esquimalt and Nanaimo Railway Company, is really a Canadian Pacific Railway Company bill, as they own the subsidiary company. Bill No. 41 contains a provision that in respect of each branch line, construction must be commenced within twc years after the passing of the bill and be completed within five years. This provisior is not contained in Bill No. 62 now before us I should certainly like to have some explanation of the omission. I suggest it would give us a good deal more confidence in the genuineness of this application if the bill contained such a provision. The clause is embodied in other Canadian Pacific Railway bills, and at least its spirit is to be found in the Canadian National Railway bills, but their lines have to 'be completed within tjhree years.
The hon. member for Nanaimo has said that no other railway is likely to go into the territory to be served by these proposed branch lines, the inference being, then why have any hesitation about granting possibly a very lengthy renewal of this charter. But some-
