times things move very quickly, and there has been such a rapid development in the west that we do not know what may happen in another ten years. We have seen many railways built by the Canadian National in '.he last decade that were not even dreamed of before that period. And it is possible that before another five years have elapsed we may see the Canadian National Railway knocking at our doors.
But there is another feature in this connection. I have in my hand the votes and proceedings of the British Columbia legislature for January 29, 1929, and I find there the member for the local district, Mr. Hanna, asking the government what their intentions are with regard to building a highway from Alberni to the west coast of Vancouver island at or near Tofino, which is practically the route covered by this bill. The government reply, as usual, that the project is under consideration; )but they also say that they have had a survey made. This I think indicates that the matter is genuinely under the consideration of the British Columbia government. Of course if undertaken the road would be built as a tourist and settlement road, and at a large cost. I think the estimate is something like four hundred thousand dollars, and undoubtedly before the road was finished it would probably cost a great deal more. In these days we are looking towards motor bus transportation, 'both passenger and freight, and it may be that the provincial government contemplates granting a charter to a bus company to assist the building of the highway. Governments are notoriously anxious and always willing to find excuses for not spending money, and it may be that the government would be glad to say, "We did contemplate genuinely enough building tlm highway but when we found that the Canadian Pacific Railway, through parliament at Ottawa, undertook to construct a railway on this same route it did not become us to bother about the matter". So that it might actually militate against the success of those who want the road, and we might not get either railway or highway inasmuch as both parties would be waiting, one on the other.
Of course, if the railway is going to go on, the whole ground is wiped from under my feet. I should be glad indeed if that were the case. But I recall what happened in the case of the settlers in the Peace River. They settled, fully expecting-indeed they were promised-that railway transportation would be provided; but it was not and the people were simply starved out. Pitiful tales could be told of what happened to those settlers,
[Mr. Neill.l
and I do not want the same thing to happen in connection with this interior road from Alberni to the. west coast. Settlers are not learned in the law and do not understand that a bill which states ostensibly that a road is going to be built does not necessarily guarantee the construction of that road. An hon. gentleman opposite had a similar bill before parliament six years ago. I brought up the same point, that the settlers had been waiting for the railway and were entitled to have it built, and someone observed rather callously, "It is up to the settlers to take care of themselves." But I submit that the settlers are not in a position to take care of themselves. They are told by the colonizing agent in the old country that a road will be built, that the charter has been granted; and they think that the charter means a guarantee of the building of the road. On the strength of this they go into these remote places where there are no transportation facilities, and they are obliged to carry their flour and other stores on their backs. Notwithstanding that they have been promised that a railway will be constructed, and in view of such promise have taken their wives and families into these distant places, nothing is done and they are starved out. I want to avoid that in connection with this railway and to make sure that nothing of the kind will happen here. I do not want settlers to go into this district believing that a railway is to be built if there is no reasonable guarantee of construction.
The second point I wish to discuss in connection with the bill is this: there is no provision for bonds; that is to say, there is nothing providing for the money for the construction of the road. Even the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, wealthy corporation as it is, will not tackle an expenditure of a couple of millions without having provision for bonding privileges. Let me explain the point as well as I can. I am not a lawyer, and it may seem presumptuous for me to raise such a point. But it is not so much a question of law as of fact and common sense, of which even lawyers have not a monopoly. Indeed, one of the most celebrated lawsuits in the old country had its origin in the fact that an able and eminent judge had drawn his own will and made a mess of it. I want to explain how it comes about that there are no bonding privileges. The original act was passed in 1919, being section 83 of the statutes of that date; and section 4 of that act provided for bonding privileges. I need not read it; it provides that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company may issue securities not exceeding $50,000 a mile. That act was

Esquimalt and Nanaimo Railway
assented to on June 6, 1919. I particularly call attention to the date, June 6, because a good deal hinges upon it. That, I say, was the year 1919. Provision was made to begin construction within two years, completion in five years; the act provides that the privileges granted would lapse if the road were not built within five years after its passage. Now it is a well known point in law that an act is passed and goes into effect only when it is assented to; previously to that it is a bill and may be withdrawn or defeated. Five years from June 6, 1919, would be June 6, 1924. I have no doubt that the company intended to come to the house and obtain a renewal of the charter; and as a matter of fact it did. It came to parliament in 1924. I have the act before me. But they made what I regard as two slips in the drafting of it. First of all, they did not amend the old act, providing that the act should stand, and merely altering the date, which would be in accordance with the custom followed in amending such acts. They did not do that; they simply partially reenacted the measure. They said, "We are going to build the railway," and they re-stated in part the terms of the act. The second mistake was that they forgot to reenact the bonding clause. They put in a clause giving power to build the railway, but they did not reenact section 4 which deals with bonding privileges.
Is this company owned and controlled by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company?

It is owned and controlled
by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.

They would not need
bonding privileges to build a road like that.
I think they would.

They had it in 1919.

They could build it with
their own funds.

But it is not in accordance
with the custom. At any rate, they themselves secured the bonding privilege in 1919. If the hon. gentleman says that they carry around a couple of millions loose in their pockets, and if they are satisfied to build it with cash funds, I suppose we have nothing to say. But the point I am making is this: I want to see this road built, and I do not want to have any flaw in the act. I have no doubt that what they intended in the act of 1924 was to revive the old act of 1919, which provided bonding privileges. But owing to
the passage of time and the extent to which members talked in those days they did not get the act of 1924 assented to until the 19th day of July of that year, six weeks after the old act had lapsed. And of course you cannot revive an act. You can have it re-enacted. Well, they did re-enact the act but, as I have explained, they failed to re-enact the bonding privilege clause, which consequently is no longer in existence.
I should doubt it very much.

Possibly it is a point for
lawyers to argue, but I am anxious to see that no flaw shall creep into this bill. I do not wish, two or three or five years from now, to have the question asked why the railway has not been built and then be told that there was some slip in the bill and that no bonding privilege was provided. I merely throw out this suggestion, and no doubt the hon. member in charge of the bill will consider the point. I am not offering anything in the nature of destructive criticism.	_	_
Another suggestion I wish to submit is this. I see no reason whatever why this railway should not come in the ordinary course under the Railway Act, so far as section 161 is concerned. The Railway Act was intended to consolidate the legislation and provide one standard act, bringing all railway charters within its scope. I do not know why, I have never been told, and I cannot conceive why this company should be made an exception.

Is that section excepted in
the original act?

It is excepted, and it is
excepted in this act by a few words at the end of section 1, which provides: "If the said railway lines are not so completed", and so forth. It is held that the insertion of these words vitiates section 161 of the Railway Act. In fact it is so admitted, and a special act always overrides the original. There is no justification for it, and if this provision were left out then the railway would come under the operation of section 161, which provides for the bona fide commencement of the work. Section 121 of the Railway Act prescribes that commencement of construction shall mean the expenditure of 15 per cent of the total cost, or of the bonding privileges, or something to that effect.

Has any work been started
on the railway up to the present time?

Eleven miles have been built under the charter of 1919, but nothing has been built of whait is now proposed by the bill.

But do I understand that
nothing has been done under the present act since 1924?

Nothing has been built of
what is now proposed, and I ask that these words be omitted, so that the Railway Act as it applies to other railways shall apply there. In that case we should have a guarantee of bona fide construction within two years and completion within five. If they once fulfil the commencement requirements there will be no danger of the road not being completed.
I propose to vote for the second reading of the bill, but I would suggest to the hon. member in charge of it that before the bill comes before the railway committee he get in touch with his principals and make the suggestions I have enumerated. He might suggest beginning the construction in two years; he might call their attention to that question of the bonding privileges which at least is doubtful and which might be easily remedied by inserting a clause in this bill, and also suggest that section 1 be amended.

After studying the course
of my motion I find I am in somewhat of a
quandary to know whether I have been ignominiously defeated or whether, on the other hand, I have achieved a very signal victory.
A short time ago I thought the majority of the hon. members of the house were very definitely against the principle contained in my motion, bult there seemed to be some black magic connected with the subamendment of the member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) for suddenly the atmosphere seems to have cleared and I find everyone in the house quite favourable to my motion as amended. As suggestions were made during the course of the debate that there was something rather sinister in my introducing this motion, I would like to read to the house two planks from the platform on which my colleague from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) and myself were elected to this house. The first plank was as follows:
Regaining for the use of the people of this country the natural resources which have been so recklessly alienated by incompetent or venal administration.
The second plank follows very naturally from the first, and is as follows:
Public ownership and democratic operation Oif pulblic utilities; and as soon as possible of essential large scale industry.
Our little group has tried to stand consistently for these principles, and when another of the great natural resources was alienated last summer I felt that we had to do what we could to protest against it; hence my motion. As I said before, I gave notice of this motion to the clerk of the house some months ago and I had then of course no idea that a commission would be investigating the situation in Manitoba at the time my motion would be introduced in the house. Notwithstanding what the members of the government have said, I still regard my motion as being quite a sensible one. I admit it has been quite easy to ridicule it by enumerating the details which would be involved in carrying it out. I tried to anticipate objections of that kind by showing that we could handle all these small transactions as we handle so many of the details in the estimates-the minister could lay on the table schedules of the transactions which had taken place in his department during the preceding year. I was not concerned in these small matters, but I believed that in view of the great value of the natural resources of this country the time had come when the water-powers, the lands and the mines should not be in the gift of the administration; their disposal should be sub-

speechtext:
If those legislatures would do that, undoubtedly it would meet the objections which I have just now voiced. I am somewhat consoled with regard to the whole matter in that after this lengthy debate, after the opinions which have been expressed on all sides of the house and in the newspapers, I really do not think either the federal government or the governments of the three prairie provinces would dare to undertake the kind of thing that was done in connection with the Seven Sisters. To that extent possibly we have made a very considerable advance.
I do not want to go into the general subject that was discussed just before the house rose by the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church), that is, the advantages of public ownership. I would, however, like to say that the advantage of public ownership is what lies behind in my mind1 all the time in urging parliamentary control. I believe in public ownership and I believe parliamentary control over these resources is at least a safeguard, because we can discuss things in the open, and public sentiment is growing so rapidly with regard to the necessity of public ownership that I think the government would be taking big risks if it defied parliament or the legislative assemblies of the country. After the speech recently delivered by the Premier of Ontario with regard to the dangers to public ownership in the propaganda which was being carried on across this country, I think we can fairly well rest assured that at least none of the western governments or this government would dare to take any course inimical to the principle of public ownership.
I recall a statement made years ago by Robert M. LaFollette in Madison Square Garden, New York, when he compared public and private ownership. He referred to the lighting of the Niagara bridge, half of that bridge being under the jurisdiction of the Dominion authorities and other half being under the jurisdiction of the United States authorities. On the Canadian side we had the Ontario hydro; on the American side the private companies. On the American side the charge for lighting for a certain period was $43 while on the Canadian side it was $8.43. That is, it was five times as much on the American half of the bridge as it was on the Canadian half. The same waters flow underneath the bridge and there are the same possibilities of developing hydro, yet under a public ownership system the cost was only one-fifth of what it was under the privately owned system.
I would refer once more to a warning given out from the United States. I take it that along many of these lines what the United States is to-day, Canada is apt to be tomorrow and therefore we ought to be very careful to avoid some of the dangers into which the United States have come. Governor Pinohot in his message of transmittal, introducing the report of the Grant Power Survey Board of 1925, said:
As Pennsylvania and the nation deal with electric power, so shall we and our descendants
698	COMMONS
Natural Resources-Mr. Woodsworth
be free men, masters of our own destinies and our own souls, or we shall be the helpless servants of the most widespread, far-reaching and penetrating monopoly ever known. Either we must control electric power, or its masters and owners will control us.	.
That which is so profoundly true in the United States is equally true in Canada. They have largely lost, at least for a good many years, the opportunities of controlling their great water-powers. We still have the opportunities within our reach, and I hope we shall not fail to take advantage of the opportunities that are still ours. I suppose, since the government accepts the subamendment, it will undoubtedly pass; it will hardly be necessary for any of us to record our votes. I do not see how we could very well vote against it, but it contains only a part of what I had hoped we might be able to secure from the house. I should like to see the principle established with regard, not merely to the water-powers of the three prairie provinces but to all the water-powers in Canada.

speechtext: What has this parliament to do with the water-powers in the other provinces of Canada?

speechtext: That is a very large order.

speechtext: It is not so simple as the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) may think. The fathers of confederation were thinking in terms of line fences, of surveys, of corner-posts. In the meantime, we have developed our rivers. They had the rivers then, and as soon as they eame to talk about those which passed provincial boundaries, there was the recognition even then of the larger concerns involved. I submit that when it comes to water-powers, we touch interests that are not merely local in their character.

There may have
been some mention of them; I have not the act here, and I cannot recall the words. I quite admit that even at that time there were certain powers. Under the British North America Act all the matters of local importance were to be left in the hands of the provinces. But I do not think I misinterpret the spirit of the British North America Act when I say that there was also present the thought of matters that were of general interest to the country at large. But I am not interpreting the British North America Act to-night. I had no idea of going into that question except to suggest that there were certain powers which even under the British North America Act were left to the Dominion of Canada, and in view of the advances which have been made in water-power development I think we may very well consider whether the water-powers on the St. Lawrence are entirely a provincial matter. I do not think that this can be taken for granted as the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George seems to consider is the case. I think there is a wider interpretation possible even there.
But there are other powers located outside the organized provinces, and it was all this that I had in view when I said that I had hoped that the general principle would be taken into consideration to-night, and that we would concede that we ought not to deal with matters of this kind without reference to parliament itself. Of course, we cannot tie each provincial legislature; I am not suggesting that, but I would hope, so far as the western provinces are concerned, that they will adopt the principle which we have urged, namely parliamentary control of the disposal of our natural resources.

Natural Resources-Mr. Bourassa

speechtext:
My
hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) in opening his remarks this evening said that he felt himself to be in a quandary. I ought to be in a deeper quandary, for the reason that I have followed very little of this debate. Perhaps, for the same reason, I shall be in a position to give, if not a more intelligent vote, at, least one less perturbed by many of the considerations and side issues brought up during this debate. For example, I do not propose, sir, to have anything to do with the Seven Sisters. I still feel too young to come so close to ladies of that character, especially after they have been handled in such a manner by politicians of all parties.
With regard to the three motions before us, it seems to me that my good friend from Winnipeg North Centre has not quite realized the effect of the subamendment proposed by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens); and the government having apparently decided to accept that proposition, I do not think that they, either, have quite realized its bearing. My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre has suggested that this proposition should be adopted unanimously. Once more, I feel myself a little more Irish than the Irish: I am both "agin" the government and "agin" the opposition in this matter.
If I understand aright the proposition of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, it is a very simple one, a broad one, and one open to fair discussion. He lays down as a general principle of legislation that none of the natural resources, no part of the domain of the crown as vested in the right of the Dominion, should be disposed of until such disposition is ratified by parliament. That suggests the great and far-reaching principle of the paramount authority of parliament over government. If the subamendment proposed by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre is accepted, we at once divest ourselves of that authority which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre wants to strengthen. Besides, we divest this government, and this government consents to be divested, of the powers of administration that havp heretofore been vested in them by parliament and by the constitution of Canada. So that, as a matter of fact, the motion of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre is the very negation in principle and in practice of the motion proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Does not the subamendment merely propose to vest the power in the
provincial legislatures, which have real jurisdiction over their own rights?

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will
allow me, I am not preparing to enter into a legal argument with a lawyer of his ability.
I am speaking simply as a parliamentarian, with a certain degree of experience, and some knowledge of the principles of parliamentary government. I am not discussing whether the motion or the amendment is right or wrong. I am simply saying that I cannot see how anyone who is in favour of the motion presented by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre can be in favour of the motion offered as a substitute by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, because it seems to me that one is the complete negation in principle and in practice of the other. That is my first point.
My second point is that the subamendment is also very different from the amendment proposed by the acting leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie). I leave it to the hon. gentleman and the hon. member for Vancouver Centre to compose their differences of opinion in that respect.
With regard to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, as he knows, much as I have of personal regard for him, as a parliamentarian I do not quite trust him. This is not the first time that he has succeeded-I compliment him for his ability-in getting this government to renounce its policy in favour of one offered to it by himself. So far as that is concerned he deserves much credit; but I do not think the so-called Liberal government deserves much credit for accepting an amendment offered to it by the hon.* member for Vancouver Centre, not because it comes from the hon. member, but because of the manner in -which it is presented, and also of what it leads to. I think it is a very weak attitude on the part of the government..
Let us go further. What will be the effect in practice not only as regards the three western provinces, but as regards the whole Dominion of Canada if this motion is accepted?
I leave the legal lights of this chamber to decide whether or not the government has the right to divest itself of these or any powers, held and exercised heretofore under the constitution, and to hand them over to provincial governments. I have been told time and again by the legal officers of the crown, and by eminent barristers as well, that neither the federal government can invest the provincial governments nor can the provincial governments invest the federal government
700	COMMONS
Natural Resources-Mr. Bourassa
with any of their respective powers. I simply cite their authority for that statement; I express no opinion upon it.
Now, by this amendment it is proposed to put the three provinces, Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan, in the same position in which the government of British Columbia has been put by a certain piece of legislation which, I confess, I read for the first time ten minutes ago. But remembering the origin of this legislation, I am struck first with one basic difference as to the situation in British Columbia and the situation in the prairie provinces. British Columbia, as we all know, came into confederation as a fully-fledged province, just as the maritime provinces and United Canada had come in. The domain of the crown, including water-powers and everything else, was vested in the crown in right of the province of British Columbia; but by subsequent legislation the province consented to hand over to the federal government a certain piece of land in return for the disbursements made by the federal government under the authority of the federal parliament for the construction of the Canadian Pacific railway. So, when this act of 1912 was passed, the federal parliament was simply handing back to British Columbia a part of the rights which that province had given to the Dominion in 1884. This is entirely different from what we are asked to do now, that is, to prejudice, so to speak, the settlement of that great problem of the handing over to those three provinces the natural resources contained within their territory. To those resources the provinces may have a moral title; but as a matter of fact they never held them under any statute or under the constitution of Canada. So you see, Mr. Speaker, there is already apparent a very deep difference, both in principle, in law and in practice, as between the situation created in British Columbia by the act of 1912 and the situation which we propose to create by a stroke of the pen at the suggestion of the member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) to be wielded by his followers, the members of the Liberal government!
Now there is another point which my bon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre made a moment ago. I think it is a very strong point, and we should ponder it a little before we legislate unanimously upon this motion. The point is this. We are called upon to decide that no further disposition-I interject this: of any nature, for any purpose whatever, for any public right or interest whatever- shall be made by the federal authorities. The parliament of Canada, invested by the people

with the responsibility of safeguarding the public interest, will now decide, by a stroke of the pen, as to the disposal, for any purpose whatever, of an asset that, as the Prime Minister said the other day, is simply the beginning of a source of industrial and economic strength and prosperity which no man in this house or outside can yet calculate. In order to arrange matters, and to put an end to an annoying debate, we are going to decide to renounce for all time to come, and hand over to the three prairie provinces -with whom this government has not been able to come to terms on the very principle upon which this is based-we are going to dispose, I say, on the spur of the moment, of what may become in the future one of the most valuable assets for the people of those provinces as well as for the people of Canada at large.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman a question there? Why would he condemn the people who make up the western provinces to a different handling of their water-power resources from what he now argues on behalf of the province of Quebec?

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Not at all. Perhaps I did not make myself clear to my hon. friend. I made no mention of Ontario or Quebec.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: I just cited Quebec.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will be as patient wdth me as I am with him when he speaks,-although there is always this difference: he is interesting, I am not-I will explain what I mean. The point I made, first, was that before this parliament settles that big problem-and perhaps this may be a satisfactory answer to my friend-the principle upon which the western provinces are to receive their natural resources should be agreed upon. Ever since I have been in public life I have held the view, and I have expressed it in Quebec and elsewhere, that the people of Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan should be put on the same footing as the people of the other provinces with regard to natural resources or any other question having to do with national or local affairs. I do not want Canada to have "superior" and "inferior" provinces; I want them all to be equal. But has this government the right, under the direction of one member of this house, to dispose of one factor of this problem before the whole problem has been dealt with? From the broad point of view, have they the right to divest themselves of one of their powers of administra-

Natural Resources-Mr. Bourassa
tion, of which they are not the masters, but which has been confided to them by the people of Canada at large? On the other hand, as shrewd diplomats-and in a matter of this nature it is a question of diplomacy- have they the right to hand over to the party with whom they are negotiating, one of their most valuable assets? Have you ever heard in the world of diplomacy of one government giving away to the other party a part of what it has in its hands, prejudicing thereby a final 'settlement?
Now, with regard to the rest of Canada,- to my friend from Bow River I repeat, if necessary, that the people of the western provinces should be put on the same footing as the people of the eastern provinces; but I do not agree that in order to please the people of the three prairie provinces we should prejudice either the rights or the situation of the eastern provinces. This is the point to which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has directed attention, and I want to emphasize it. Of course, as he said, the water-powers and all that they are capable of giving to the people of Canada could have been nothing in the imagination of the fathers of confederation, or, to speak of actual facts, those water-powers are comparatively nothing to-day, compared with what they may be twenty-five or fifty years hence. The enormous problem of the control of these resources, for navigation purposes, for industrial purposes, for the preservation of forests by the maintenance of large areas of flooded lands, especially in that vast country extending from Labrador to lake Timiskaming-this whole problem is bound up with this question of water rights and water-powers.

speechtext:
My hon.
friend seems to be arguing as though these resources were being turned over to the provinces. Only the administration of them is affected.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
I will make myself clear. I entirely agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that this is too considerable a question to be settled solely in reference to some provision contained in some small corner of the British North America Act passed in 1867 by men of whom perhaps not one knew what water-power was, and who certainly could not foresee what water-powers would be in our day; indeed, we ourselves cannot conceive their possibilities fifty years hence. I say, therefore, whether the question is one of disposal or of administration, that we have no right to prejudice any factor of this great problem. We have no right to lay
down the principle that water-powers are any more the property of the provinces than of the Dominion. A classification will have to be made, first, from a technical standpoint and carefully studied, just as the problem of water-powers was studied and solved in Switzerland, for example, to speak of one country I know. There water-powers have been classified, first, from a purely technical point of view, then from the viewpoint of industrial possibilities, and finally handed over, some to the national government, some to the various cantons, and others to the municipalities for local needs. That policy I advocated in the legislature of Quebec twenty years ago, and while it does not make me any younger to refer to the fact, at the same time I feel now, as I felt then, that we have no right to make a gift of these powers either to Sir Herbert Holt or to the International company, as the so-called Liberal but really Tory government of Quebec is doing from week to week and from month to month. We have no right either, we the trustees of the Canadian people, to hand over all that possible wealth to the provinces, either for disposal or even simply for administration. If we vote in favour of the subamendment we commit ourselves in general, unequivocal and unreserved terms to the admission that all water-powers are of provincial interest alone. Whether we commit ourselves by the use of the word "disposal" or the word "administration", I for one, not being a lawyer, refuse to plunge headlong into this matter; I refuse to be crippled within the four comers-if one can speak in terms of dimension in this regard-of one or two words in a particular text. I always endeavour to find out the spirit and the consequence of a principle of legislation or of any determination of this house, and I have tried to read this text with that object in view. If I am right in my interpretation, it means this, that ten or twenty years hence, if this proposal is incorporated in the provincial statutes of the three provinces, if it forms a part of the final agreement with those provinces in relation to their natural resources, we shall have Ontario and Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia knocking at our door, asking us to renounce all rights and titles we may now have over any water-powers for the general interests of the people of Canada, in order to give these provincial governments the opportunity of handling those resources in the interests of their own people, who after all are but fractions of the nation as a whole, but possibly also to hand them over to a handful of sharks, as has been done in the province of Quebec for the last
702	COMMONS
Natural Resources-Mr. Bourassa
twenty years. I am not prepared to associate my name with any such proposal, the consequences of which I foresee.
For the last twenty years I have fought in the province of Quebec against both Liberals and Tories because of the manner in which they have dealt with the public domain of that province. Some of us succeeded after many years in getting the government of that province to do something to preserve the forests of the country; but so far as water-powers are concerned, there has been an orgy of favoritism, which is disquieting not only to thinking people, but to all enlightened men associated with industry and water-power development. I have myself heard this from one of the directors of a large company: "We don't know whither we are going, but we are obliged to take more than we can handle, because if we do not, the government will give it to the other concern." For that reason one large concern grabs all it can of forest reserves and water-powers, the object being to prevent the rival interest from obtaining these resources. That is a pretty clear illustration of what may ensue if we once lay down the principle and, for the sake of a bonne entente between warring parties in this house, thus compromise the future. It may be said that any act we pass now may be repealed. Well, I hope my good friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) will forgive me if I venture to suggest that I have read somewhat more extensively in history than he has, for the simple reason that I have had more leisure. And my reading, not only of Canadian history but of the history of many nations, convinces me that once a government divests itself of a given power it becomes impossible, especially in a so-called democratic electoral country, and more particularly in a confederation, for the central authority to resume control once it has lost it, or to take back anything it has given up. Why? Because the sense of public opinion, if you like, or the opposition of so-called vested interests, or, if you will, the feeling, laudable in itself, of respect for provincial rights, will render it impossible. Let my good friends of the government rest assured of this: If they support this proposal before us, they will never regain what they give up; they will be forced to disgorge everything that belongs to the people of Canada, of whom they are the mandatories and servants. And, what is more, they will be forced to do for the other provinces what they are doing in this connection. That is my deep and serious reason for not accepting the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens).

With regard to the motion itself, I may say to my good friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that although I am generally pleased to vote with him I cannot agree with his resolution. It may be good in principle, but a single thought is sufficient to demonstrate that in practice it would handicap the functioning of government. The hon. member for Melfort (Mr. McLean), in a most practical manner, has demonstrated that if this principle of legislation had been adopted twenty years ago there would probably be no population in the western provinces to-day. I have known the western provinces for a longer time than many of those who represent them to-day. I travelled through that country thirty or more years ago, and then as now the people were grumbling against the handicapping of the federal administration; they were grumbling against the Canadian Pacific Railway and its servant, the parliament of Canada; grumbling at the Department of tihe Interior, the Department of Immigration, the Department of Indian Affairs. And it always came back to this objection: "Those men in Ottawa are too far away to know our problems." That is one of the reasons why I was converted to the idea of handing over the administration of the whole of these lands of the west, long before my good friend from Bow River crossed the ocean to become the excellent and distinguished Canadian he now is.
But precisely because I want the people of the west to deal with what is their own, or what will be their own after this question is settled, not piecemeal but according to principle and practice, I cannot accept the motion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre either in principle or in practice. It is true that governments in this country as in England, the United States, France and elsewhere, have freed themselves of their moral responsibility to parliament; it is true that governments in this country under all regimes have done things behind the back of parliament which they should not have done. I think a couple of years ago I quoted the opinion once expressed by Lecky as to the abnormal authority now monopolized by the cabinet under the British system of government. So, from that point of view, I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre; but when it comes to a partition as between broad principles of legislation and matters of management, I must confess that I believe, and always have believed, that democracy and parliamentary government is t failure. Keep control over the principle of new law; keep control over the men who govern the country and punish them if they

Natural Resources-Mr. Edwards (Frontenac)
do wrong; but give them ample opportunity to administer; because if you force them to come before parliament with every small act of administration; if you force the Minister of the Interior to report to parliament the sale of every section or quarter-section of land in the we^t or of every bit of forest, while perhaps you may spare the country a few misdeeds-although I am not quite sure that parliament as a whole is much superior to the government as a whole, either in point of morality or in point of competency-you will hamper them to a very large degree.

No. As far as management is concerned I am prepared to trust this government; I would trust hon. gentlemen opposite the moment the people of Canada thought fit, rightly or wrongly, to trust them, and as long as they were the government. I do not think they should come here, lose their time and make us lose our time, in rendering account foT every action taken by every department; but I would hold them hard and fast to the principles of our constitution and to the sound principles of government as they exist in every country. I would see that in connection with every bit of legislation brought down they do their duty by the people of Canada, and then trust them with small matters or even large matters of administration.
For all these reasons, sir, I find myself to be in opposition to the opposition; I find myself to be in opposition to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and in opposition to the government. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I shall require but a very short time for the few observations I have to make and which I am privileged to make because of the subamendment. speechtext: I will leave them to you; they are in need of a good doctor.

speechtext:
I thought, Mr. Speaker, I was to have the floor after
the hon. member for Labelle had finished, but evidently the hon. member is not through until he is outside the door. I was about to remark that I was sure those ladies, the Seven Sisters, would very deeply appreciate the reticence of the hon. member for Labelle in leaving them severely alone, and probably if they could be vocal would express their deep gratitude at their escape.
The hon. member for Labelle has paid a high compliment to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens); in the estimation of the hon. gentleman the government is at present on this side of the house in the person of my genial friend from Vancouver Centre.
In the course of the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) this afternoon I noticed two things in particular: First he spoke about getting some person on this side out of a dilemma, and he immediately followed that remark by the statement that it was his intention and the intention of the government to support the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre. Such tenderness of heart and such solicitude on the part of the right hon. gentleman for those who sit on this side of the house is extremely rare. There seemed to be a little dispute between the two sides of the house as to who was in a dilemma ; on this side certain persons evidently wanted to get the government out of a hole, while the government was equally eager to get those on this side of the house out of a hole. I do not know where it is going to end, but I predict that if this sort of thing continues very long this session will be over long before Easter. I do think, however, from my knowledge of politics, that this throwing of bouquets and this kindness of heart manifested on each side spells danger for the Dominion of Canada.
The hon. member who has just vacated his seat and run out (Mr. Bourassa) said that the province of British Columbia entered into union as a full-fledged province, and in that respect was very different from the prairie provinces. Well, at least that is an admission on his part that the prairie provinces are not full-fledged, or in other words that they are not provinces at all up to the present. I was surprised, and I may say somewhat pleased, to hear .the hon. member for Labelle state that he wanted to see the prairie provinces given equality of status with the other provinces of the Dominion. I did not gather that that was his attitude toward the prairie provinces in 1926, from what he said on January 29 of that year; I came to a very different

Natural Resources-Mr. Edwards (Frontenac)
conclusion, then, and I believe the people of Canada came to a different conclusion at that time as to his attitude towards the prairie provinces.
When I rose, Mr. Speaker, I said I did not intend to take up very many minutes of the time of the house, but I should like to refer to some remarks made during the course of this debate by that eminent jurist, that man who some day probably will be Chief Justice of Canada or occupy some other high position on the bench. I refer to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston).

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: More bouquets.

speechtext:
Well, hon.
gentlemen opposite can contemplate the bouquet as it is now and- then look at it a little later. During the course of his remarks the other day the Minister of National Defence said that he could not, either as a member of the house or as a professional man, agree with the legal opinion expressed by myself. I was not aware that I had expressed any legal opinion. I did quote extensively from those who, I thought, were well qualified to express legal opinions, and if the Minister of National Defence had any confidence in his attainments as a lawyer he would have replied to the arguments I presented rather than directed his remarks to myself personally. I can assure him that he is entirely wrong in saying that I put myself up as the chief justice of the court of constitutional principles. I would not presume to do that because I have not the legal knowledge which would fit me for that position. Even though I had the legal knowledge I would not put myself in the field against the possible attainment of his ambitions for a position which, if he ever gets it, I hope he will fill better than the one he is in now. I desire to direct the attention of the Minister of National Defence to some words he used the other day, and which I was very much surprised to read in Hansard. He said:
I do not think the western provinces will associate themselves with the contention he made,-
-referring to myself.
-which was to this effect: It is true that when we came into eonfedration we got a certain payment in lieu of lands, but we now find that you had no right constitutionally and technically to withhold our lands; therefore we suggest that we should have the money in lieu of lands and the lands too.
Those are the sentiments he credits to me as having expressed in the course of my remarks. He then continued:

That was the argument of the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington, and I only desire to go on record as stating that I cannot agree with any such contention.
Every hon. member who was present when I introduced my resolution, to which every hon. member agreed including the Minister of National Defence, knows that I never made use of any such words, nor did I make use of any words which by the wildest stretch of imagination could be twisted into the construction placed upon them by the minister. I want to say to the minister that as a minister of the crown it should be beneath his dignity to resort to methods of that kind. The minister has shown a disposition at various times in his political career to be anything but fair and to be absolutely unjust when it comes to dealing with matters in a political way. Apparently it is utterly impossible for the Minister of National Defence to divest himself of his political coat and his extreme partisanship in discussing any question in the house in which he is interested. The minister cannot find in my remarks the sentiments which he placed in my mouth, nor will he find them in the remarks I made in introducing my resolution, and my reason in speaking now is to draw that fact to his attention.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
With the permission of the house I will read the motion as it would read when amended by the amendment and the amendment to the amendment:
That, in the opinion of this house, no further disposition of the water-powers, under the control of the federal government in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta shall be made under the Dominion Water Powers Act but the said water-powers shall be administered by the respective provinces under powers to be granted by this parliament similar to the powers granted to the province of British Columbia to administer the water-powers in the railway belt as set forth in the Railway Belt Water Act of 1912, and being chapter 211 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927.

Having taken part in the debate as the seconder of the original motion I think I have the right at this stage to make a few comments upon the question which is now before the house. The debate during the last few days has made it abundantly apparent that it is almost impossible to have a question discussed before the house on its merits. The question as presented to the house by the mover of the original motion was very clear, very specific, but no sooner was the motion before the house than the clouds of political animosity and contention began to descend and before the house knew where it was the original motion had been lost sight if. The principle as set forth in the original motion was clean-cut; there was no equivocation of any kind. In my former speech I adhered strictly to the motion before the house, and I endeavoured to impress the house with the first-rate importance of the principle involved, namely, that the wealth of the people as represented in our natural resources could not rightly be disposed of by governor in council without the ratification of parliament.
The debate having gone so far I am more convinced than ever of the value of that proposition. It seems to me when any matter that relates to the interest of the people is advanced on the floor of the house, there is straightway introduced the question of provincial rights, and an abstract discussion ensues which obscures the plain rights of the people to what is theirs. I am not concerned about these abstract rights with regard to which certain members of the house become excited. I do not see how the settlement of 78594-45
this natural resources question is going to put any bread into the mouths of the common people in my constituency. I can see at this stage of the debate that the question of provincial rights has been raised over and over again in order to obscure what I call popular rights. I am not going to be a party to proclaiming the sacredness of provincial rights to the detriment of what I consider to be the only valuable right of the people, that is, their right to the possession of their natural resources or to a say in their disposal. I have heard all I want to hear about provincial rights. There is no nourishment in that dry bone for a single Manitoba farmer or workingman. There may be in it an occasion for mental gymnastics on the part of constitutional lawyers in the house and elsewhere, but when the question has been discussed as many times as it has been in the house, the people of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta are going to be exactly where they were before, with the Seven Sisters gone, and all the rest of our natural resources will go in the same direction while the representatives of the people are indulging in high-brow discussions in regard to what they call provincial rights. I was not surprised that the debate should take that course, for one has not been in the house a few years without finding that whenever an attempt is made to benefit the people on the lower levels, somebody jumps in, intervenes, with this question of provincial rights, and anything proposed in the house scarcely ever gets to the people except in a maimed and imperfect fashion. I could mention old age pensions, unemployment insurance and many other things which you cannot bring on the floor of the house without somebody intervening with the old gag about provincial rights. It is time that we were finished with this discussion of abstract rights which have no relation whatever to the welfare of the people. What I want to know is how we are going to get the Seven Sisters falls back into the possession of the people of Manitoba. If we cannot do that, I want to know how we are going to prevent the repetition of that sort of thing in our province. I do not want to hear about provincial rights; I want to hear about the rights of the men and women in Manitoba.
I was not surprised that this provincial rights debate should arise in certain quarters of the house, but I was surprised to find it come from the lips of the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Glen). I was surprised that at- a point in the debate when there was an opportunity of carrying a motion that

I am not concerned any more about the Seven Sisters; I am not concerned about the actual possession by the people of their own property; I am concerned about this abstract thing, this matter of provincial rights, and therefore I cannot support the motion." Mr. Speaker, it seems that we have been travelling in circles in this matter. It reminds me of the boys who went out 'coon hunting; soon after they started out they got lost and wandered around all night, but in the morning they found themselves back where they had' started. It seems to me that the government omnibus has become mired; the Conservative opposition have come along with their struggle buggy and become lodged in the same mire, and this afternoon we had the spectacle of the occupants of both vehicles getting out and helping each other out of the mire.
A few years ago, in 1921, this proposition was considered of sufficient importance for the government of the day to declare it a work for the general advantage of Canada, and I well remember two debates which took place during sessions of the fourteenth parliament, one in 1922 and the other in 1923, when attempts were made to repeal that legislation. It is true that these attempts were passed by this house, but they were turned down by

Natural Resources-Mr. Fansher
the senate on both occasions. However, I believe that last year this legislation was repealed; in other words, the government had no sooner divested themselves of the right to claim that this was a work for the general advantage of Canada than they seemed to feel that this power could be given away to a private corporation. I would like to quote a few sentences from the speech made by the then leader of the opposition during the debate of 1923, appearing at page 4166 of the debates of that year:
Hon. members, of course, know that in the provisions of the British North America Act the parliament of Canada has power to declare any works to be for the general advantage of the Dominion, works which presumably theretofore were works over which the provinces had legislative jurisdiction. That power on the part of the parliament of Canada is unrestrained, but in practice is exercised wherever the works are such as affect the people of more than one province, where the works are such that, in the judgment of parliament, federal legislative control is preferable to provincial control.
Further on he said:
I urged then, as I urge now, that these are works that ought to be declared to be works for the general advantage of Canada, because they really are works for the general advantage of Canada. We have declared over and over again a few miles of railway wholly within a province to be a work ffir the general advantage of Canada. Here are works as respects which the province of Manitoba, though the works are in Ontario, is perhaps even more interested than the latter province. The power assets that the flow of the water constitutes are, to the extent I think of about 80 per cent, in the province of Manitoba, and the future commercial development of Manitoba is dependent upon the just and equitable legislative administration of those works. I repeat what I said a year ago: If there ever were works that ought to be declared works for the general advantage of Canada, that are appropriate for such declaration, these are the very works.
Those were the words of Right Hon. Arthur Meighen at the time this legislation was sought to be repealed. I remember that at that time a number of members from the province of Manitoba strongly supported that stand, and no less a person than the then member for South Winnipeg, Hon. A. B. Hudson, also supported the stand taken by the leader of the opposition. He went even further in stating that these works were for the general advantage of Canada and quoted quite extensively from what had been done in Switzerland in the line of hydro-electric development.

To my mind this stand was taken because these gentlemen believed that while control was vested in this parliament these waters would not be alienated and given over to a private corporation. Hon. A. B. Hudson made quite extensive observations with regard to this matter. He stated that the property right did not pass upon the control being vested in the parliament of Canada any more than it did in the control of the fisheries by regulation; the possession of the fish did not in that ease pass from the provinces.
I was amazed to find that the opposition seemed very anxious to eliminate the Beau-harnois scheme from this resolution. We have been discussing a water-power which has been alienated; we have been crying, as it were, over spilt milk, but we are about to give another great water-power to a private corporation in the province of Quebec. I had hoped that the government of the day would give this country a lead in connection with power development, but it seems the government is taking the course of least resistance. The province of Quebec seems to be taking the lead in the development of water-powers by private interests; the government do not wish to gain their ill-will and they are agreeable to allowing the private interests to develop the power. As I understand the amendment now before the house, it is simply that whatever decision is arrived at by the legislatures of the provinces concerned, the Dominion government will turn over the water-powers to the respective provinces. It seems to me that the people's representatives in the various provinces should have an opportunity of passing upon these proposals. Water-powers are one of our most valuable resources and we can scarcely estimate their worth to the provinces or to the Dominion as a whole.
